guide.summary: Unit 4 covers the physical Earth systems that set the stage for life and human resource use: plate tectonics, soil formation and properties, the structure of the atmosphere, global wind and climate patterns, watersheds, solar radiation and seasons, rain shadows, and El Niño–Southern Oscillation.

sections.heading: Plate tectonics
sections.body: Convergent boundaries: oceanic–continental and oceanic–oceanic collisions cause subduction, deep trenches, volcanoes, and earthquakes; continental–continental collisions build mountains (Himalayas). Divergent boundaries create new crust at mid-ocean ridges and rift valleys. Transform boundaries slide past each other and produce earthquakes with little volcanism (San Andreas Fault). The Ring of Fire around the Pacific marks subduction zones.

sections.heading: Soil
sections.body: Soil forms from weathering of parent material over long periods, influenced by climate, organisms, topography, and time. Horizons: O (organic litter), A (topsoil: humus mixed with minerals), E (leached zone, in some soils), B (subsoil, where leached minerals accumulate), C (weathered parent material), R (bedrock). Texture is the percent sand, silt, and clay, read on a soil texture triangle; loam (roughly 40% sand, 40% silt, 20% clay) is ideal for agriculture. Sand has large pores and high permeability but holds little water; clay has tiny pores, holds water and nutrients, but drains slowly and can waterlog. Erosion by wind and water is accelerated by tilling, overgrazing, and deforestation.

sections.heading: Atmosphere, wind, and climate
sections.body: Layers by temperature: troposphere (weather; most of the air's mass), stratosphere (ozone layer absorbs UV, temperature rises with altitude), mesosphere, thermosphere. The atmosphere is about 78% N₂, 21% O₂, ~0.9% Ar, and ~0.04% CO₂. Unequal heating drives circulation: air rises at the equator (rain, rainforests), descends near 30° latitude (dry, deserts), and rises again near 60°. The Coriolis effect deflects winds, producing trade winds and westerlies. The equator receives more solar energy per unit area because sunlight strikes more directly; seasons result from Earth's 23.5° axial tilt, not distance from the Sun. A rain shadow forms when moist air rises over mountains, cools, and drops precipitation on the windward side; descending air warms and dries the leeward side.

sections.heading: Watersheds and ENSO
sections.body: A watershed is all the land that drains into a particular body of water. Land use anywhere in a watershed (deforestation, paving, agriculture) affects water quality and flooding downstream. In normal years, trade winds push warm surface water west across the Pacific, causing upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water off South America. During El Niño, trade winds weaken, warm water shifts east, upwelling decreases (hurting Peruvian fisheries), and rainfall patterns change (wetter western South America, drier Indonesia and Australia). La Niña intensifies normal conditions: stronger trade winds and stronger upwelling.

sections.heading: Worked example: soil analysis
sections.body: A soil sample is 40% sand, 40% silt, and 20% clay, which the soil texture triangle classifies as loam. Loam is ideal for agriculture because it balances drainage (from sand), nutrient and water retention (from clay), and workability. Soils high in clay drain poorly and can become waterlogged, while sandy soils drain quickly and lose nutrients through leaching. Soil horizons include O (organic matter), A (topsoil), B (subsoil), and C (weathered parent material).

sections.heading: Worked example: atmospheric circulation
sections.body: Uneven solar heating drives global wind patterns. Near the equator, warm moist air rises, cools, and releases precipitation, creating tropical rainforests. At about 30° latitude, dry air sinks, creating deserts. The Coriolis effect deflects winds, producing trade winds and westerlies. Rain shadows form when moist air rises over mountains, cools, and drops precipitation on the windward side, leaving the leeward side dry.

sections.heading: El Niño and La Niña
sections.body: During El Niño, trade winds weaken, warm water spreads eastward across the Pacific, upwelling off South America decreases, fisheries decline, and weather patterns shift globally. La Niña strengthens normal conditions, with stronger trade winds and more upwelling.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.body: Students confuse weather with climate, mix up convergent and divergent boundaries, and forget that clay retains water and nutrients better than sand.

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know plate boundaries, soil horizons, soil texture, permeability, porosity, atmospheric layers, Hadley cells, Coriolis effect, rain shadow, watershed, and ENSO.

sections.heading: Free-response connection
sections.body: Questions often ask you to explain how a plate boundary causes earthquakes or volcanoes, identify a soil type from data, or describe how ENSO affects weather and fisheries.

keyTakeaways: Subduction → trenches, volcanoes, earthquakes; transform → earthquakes.
Sand drains fast; clay holds water; loam is ideal.
Weather happens in the troposphere; the ozone layer is in the stratosphere.
Deserts at ~30° latitude from descending dry air.
El Niño weakens trade winds and upwelling.
commonMistakes: Attributing seasons to Earth's distance from the Sun.
Putting the rain shadow on the windward side.
Saying clay soils have high permeability.
Confusing El Niño (weak trade winds) with La Niña (strong trade winds).
Placing the ozone layer in the troposphere.
examTips: Soil texture triangle questions require reading three axes; practice tracing the lines.
Expect a diagram of a mountain range with wind direction for rain shadows.
ENSO questions focus on upwelling, fisheries, and rainfall shifts.
Investigations often measure infiltration rate or soil water-holding capacity.
guide.cramSheet:
**Plates:** convergent (subduction: trench, volcano) · divergent (ridge, rift) · transform (quakes)

**Soil:** O A E B C R · sand drains · clay holds · loam 40/40/20

**Air:** 78% N₂ · 21% O₂ · troposphere weather · stratosphere ozone

**Circulation:** rise at 0° (wet) · sink at 30° (deserts) · Coriolis

**Seasons:** tilt 23.5° · direct sun at equator

**Rain shadow:** windward wet · leeward dry

**ENSO:** El Niño weak trades, less upwelling · La Niña stronger

vocab.definition: One tectonic plate sinking beneath another at a convergent boundary.
A boundary where plates slide horizontally past one another.
A distinct layer of soil with characteristic properties.
Decomposed organic matter in topsoil that holds water and nutrients.
How easily water moves through soil.
Soil with a balanced mix of sand, silt, and clay, ideal for agriculture.
The lowest atmospheric layer, where weather occurs.
Deflection of moving air or water caused by Earth's rotation.
A dry area on the leeward side of a mountain range.
All the land that drains into a particular body of water.
Rise of cold, nutrient-rich deep water to the surface.
A periodic weakening of Pacific trade winds that warms the eastern Pacific and reduces upwelling.

practice.stem: Which features are most associated with an oceanic plate subducting beneath a continental plate?

choices.text: A rift valley and lava plains
A mid-ocean ridge and new crust
Two plates sliding past each other with no volcanoes
A deep trench and a chain of volcanoes

practice.explanation: Subduction forms a trench; the descending plate melts, feeding volcanoes on the overriding plate.

practice.stem: In which layer of the atmosphere do nearly all weather events occur?

choices.text: Stratosphere
Troposphere
Mesosphere
Thermosphere

practice.explanation: The troposphere contains most of the atmosphere's mass and water vapor.

practice.stem: Compared with clay soil, sandy soil has

choices.text: higher permeability and lower water-holding capacity
lower permeability and higher water-holding capacity
higher nutrient-holding capacity
smaller particles

practice.explanation: Large sand particles leave large pores, so water drains quickly and little is retained.

practice.stem: Earth's seasons are caused primarily by

choices.text: the tilt of Earth's axis relative to its orbit
changes in Earth's distance from the Sun
changes in the Sun's energy output
ocean currents

practice.explanation: The 23.5° tilt changes the angle of sunlight and day length through the year.

distractors.B: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in the Northern Hemisphere's winter.

practice.stimulus: Moist air from the ocean moves east across a coastal mountain range. City W lies on the west slope; City E lies in the valley east of the mountains.
practice.stem: Which statement best describes the two cities' climates?

choices.text: City E is wetter, because air collects moisture as it crosses the mountains.
City W is wetter, because rising air cools and condenses; City E is drier, because descending air warms and absorbs moisture.
Both receive equal rainfall.
City W is drier because it faces the ocean wind directly.

practice.explanation: Orographic lift drops precipitation on the windward side; the leeward side lies in a rain shadow.

practice.stem: A soil sample contains 40% sand, 40% silt, and 20% clay. On a soil texture triangle, it is classified as

choices.text: sand
clay
silt
loam

practice.explanation: A balanced mixture near 40/40/20 falls in the loam region.

practice.stem: Many of the world's large deserts lie near 30° N and 30° S latitude because

choices.text: dry air that lost its moisture near the equator descends and warms there
warm, moist air rises there, producing heavy rain
those latitudes receive the most direct sunlight
ocean currents are coldest there

practice.explanation: Hadley cell air rises at the equator, rains out, then sinks near 30°, warming and drying.

practice.stem: During an El Niño event, anchovy catches off Peru typically decline because

choices.text: stronger trade winds increase upwelling, cooling the water too much
weaker trade winds reduce upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water, lowering plankton productivity
increased rainfall makes the ocean too fresh for fish
El Niño increases ocean salinity

practice.explanation: Less upwelling means fewer nutrients, fewer phytoplankton, and less food for anchovies.

distractors.A: Describes La Niña (and it would help fisheries).

practice.stem: Clearing forests in the upper portion of a watershed is most likely to cause which effect downstream?

choices.text: Increased groundwater recharge downstream
Lower river turbidity
Increased sediment in rivers and more frequent flooding
No effect, because watersheds are separate systems

practice.explanation: Without vegetation to slow runoff and hold soil, water and sediment move quickly downstream.

practice.stem: In a forest soil profile, dissolved minerals such as iron and aluminum compounds carried downward by water would most likely accumulate in the

choices.text: O horizon
A horizon
R horizon
B horizon

practice.explanation: Leaching moves minerals out of upper horizons; they accumulate in the subsoil (B horizon).

practice.stem: Which statement best explains why a square meter of ground at the equator receives more solar energy per year than a square meter near the poles?

choices.text: Sunlight strikes the equator more directly, so the same energy is concentrated on a smaller area and passes through less atmosphere.
The equator is closer to the Sun.
The equator has more cloud cover, which traps sunlight.
The poles reflect sunlight back to the equator.

practice.explanation: At low sun angles, the same beam spreads over more ground and travels through more atmosphere.

practice.stimulus:
Students pour 100 mL of water through equal volumes of three soils.

| Soil | Time to drain (s) | Water retained (mL) |
|---|---|---|
| X | 35 | 12 |
| Y | 410 | 58 |
| Z | 120 | 34 |

choices.text: Soil X has the highest clay content and is most prone to waterlogging.
Soil Y has the highest clay content and would most need drainage for crops sensitive to waterlogging.
Soil Z is pure sand.
All three soils have the same texture.

practice.explanation: Slow drainage and high retention indicate small pores: high clay content.

distractors.A: Soil X drains fastest and retains least: sandy.

practice.stem: A region experiences frequent shallow earthquakes but has no active volcanoes. Its most likely tectonic setting is

choices.text: an oceanic–oceanic convergent boundary
a hot spot
a transform boundary
an oceanic–continental subduction zone

practice.explanation: Transform boundaries grind past each other without subduction or magma generation.

practice.stimulus: Sea-surface temperature maps show the eastern equatorial Pacific 1.5 °C cooler than average and the western Pacific warmer than average. Trade winds are stronger than normal.
practice.stem: Which conditions are most likely occurring?

choices.text: El Niño, with reduced upwelling off South America
Normal conditions
La Niña, with weaker upwelling and drought in Indonesia
La Niña, with enhanced upwelling off South America and heavier rainfall in Indonesia

practice.explanation: Stronger trade winds push more warm water west, intensifying upwelling in the east and rainfall in the west.

practice.prompt:
Students want to know how land use affects how quickly rainwater soaks into soil. They push a metal ring 5 cm into the ground at three sites (an old forest, a pasture grazed by cattle, and a plowed cornfield), pour 500 mL of water into the ring, and time how long it takes to soak in. They repeat this five times at each site.

| Site | Mean infiltration time (s) |
|---|---|
| Forest | 48 |
| Grazed pasture | 310 |
| Plowed field | 95 |

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify one variable that should be held constant.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why the students repeated the measurement five times at each site.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: State a testable hypothesis for this investigation.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Explain the most likely reason infiltration is slowest in the grazed pasture.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: Explain why the forest soil absorbs water fastest.

parts.label: g
parts.prompt: Describe one environmental consequence of slow infiltration during heavy rain.

parts.label: h
parts.prompt: Propose one practice that would improve infiltration in the cornfield, and explain how it works.

rubric.description: E.g., volume of water, ring depth or size, initial soil moisture (no recent rain), same soil type or slope.
Repeated trials reduce the effect of random variation or local differences and make results more reliable.
Testable and directional, e.g., 'If soil is compacted by grazing, then infiltration time will be longer than in forest soil.'
Cattle trampling compacts soil, reducing pore space so water enters slowly.
Abundant organic matter (humus) and root channels create porous, well-structured soil.
Runoff causes erosion and carries sediment, fertilizer, or manure into streams (or increases flooding, reduces groundwater recharge).
E.g., no-till farming, cover crops, adding compost, contour plowing.
E.g., cover-crop roots and residue add organic matter and channels that increase porosity and slow runoff.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) The land use at each site (forest, pasture, plowed field).

(b) The volume of water poured (500 mL).

(c) Repeating trials reduces the effect of random variation, such as a single rock or root, making the mean more reliable.

(d) If soil has been compacted by cattle grazing, then water will take longer to infiltrate than in forest soil.

(e) Cattle trample the pasture, compacting the soil and collapsing pore spaces, so water moves into it slowly.

(f) Forest soil has a thick layer of humus and many root channels, creating large pores that let water soak in quickly.

(g) Water that cannot infiltrate runs off the surface, eroding topsoil and carrying sediment and manure into nearby streams, which increases turbidity.

(h) Plant cover crops between corn seasons. Their roots create channels and add organic matter, increasing soil porosity, and their cover slows runoff so water has time to soak in.
